coreTruths.title: Plaque biofilm is the primary cause of virtually all periodontal disease
coreTruths.broaderContext: Periodontitis is one of the two main reasons people lose teeth. Plaque drives it, which makes plaque control the highest-leverage daily habit in dentistry.
coreTruths.body:
## The microbial community shifts as inflammation deepens

Almost every form of periodontal disease starts with plaque [1]. Healthy gums carry mostly Gram-positive aerobes and facultative anaerobes. As plaque builds up and inflammation sets in, the population shifts toward anaerobes and Gram-negative species. Established periodontitis runs on anaerobic Gram-negative rods [2].

## Treatment starts with disrupting the biofilm, not antibiotics

Every plan starts with breaking up the plaque. Disrupt the biofilm and the disease backs off [3]. OHI, scaling, and root surface debridement are not extras, they are the treatment. Antibiotics are not a shortcut [4]. Surgery only comes after non-surgical control has been tried [5], because cutting tissue without sorting out plaque just rebuilds the same problem.

## Gingivitis is the early stage of bone loss

Gingivitis comes first. There is no evidence periodontitis develops without it [6]. So treating gingivitis is bone-loss prevention, not just tidying up bleeding gums. Left alone, those bleeding gums are the start of a process that can reach bone in susceptible patients.

citations.quote: The 1° aetiology of virtually all forms of periodontal disease is plaque. It exists in a biofilm at the supragingival margin and can progress subgingivally.

Clinically healthy gingivae are associated with a high proportion of Gram +ve rods and cocci which are facultatively anaerobic or aerobic. Gingivitis is associated with an ↑ number of facultative anaerobes, strict anaerobes, and an ↑ number of Gram –ve rods. Established periodontitis is associated with a majority presence of anaerobic Gram –ve rods.

Periodontal disease is an infection due to the presence of plaque biofilm, therefore, disruption of the plaque biofilm and control of plaque is the key to success. More complex Rx will always fail in the absence of effective plaque control.

There are few reasons to use antimicrobials in periodontal therapy. The plaque biofilm affects the response, concentration in gingival crevicular fluid is low, antibiotics have side effects, and there is the growing problem of antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics are not really justified for use in chronic periodontitis.
Periodontal surgery is mostly considered after a course of non-surgical debridement.

The direct association between the presence of tooth surface plaque and gingivitis has been confirmed. Gingivitis precedes periodontitis but there is no evidence to suggest that periodontitis develops in the absence of gingivitis.

coreTruths.title: Periodontal tissue destruction is host-mediated, not direct bacterial damage
coreTruths.broaderContext: Plaque triggers periodontitis but the host's immune response does the damage. That is why smoking and diabetes shape outcomes, and why they belong in the periodontal plan.
coreTruths.body:
## The host's immune response does most of the damage

Plaque triggers periodontitis. The host's own immune response does most of the actual damage [1]. Bacteria deliver virulence factors and inflammatory mediators, but the bone loss and attachment loss come from the prolonged inflammatory and immune reaction, not the bugs directly.

## Susceptibility sits with the host: smoking and diabetes are the big modifiers

Two patients with the same plaque can have very different bone loss. The difference sits with the host. The two big modifiers in real practice are smoking and poorly controlled diabetes [2], which both turn up the inflammatory volume. That is why the current diagnosis statement names risk factors alongside stage and grade, with smoking the textbook example [3].

## Therapy that ignores the host is half a treatment

Periodontal therapy that skips host risk factors is half a treatment. A smoking cessation conversation, and where it applies a quick liaison with the GP about diabetic control, belong in the periodontal plan [4], not in someone else's clinic. Cleaning a smoker's mouth without mentioning the smoking is leaving the bigger lever untouched.

citations.quote: The host response to the biofilm is meant to be protective but can also cause local tissue damage. Both inflammatory and immunologically mediated pathways can contribute to periodontal damage.

Although mild to moderate periodontitis is common, severe periodontitis affects a relatively small subset of the population. Certain risk factors such as smoking, poorly controlled diabetes, and colonization by specific bacteria at high levels have been identified.
Generalized periodontitis stage III grade B currently unstable with smoking as a risk factor.
This is where the aim is to control plaque and address modifiable risk factors (e.g. smoking cessation counselling, liaise with GMP if poorly controlled diabetes).

coreTruths.title: Oral health is a balanced ecosystem; disease is dysbiosis, not infection by an invader
coreTruths.broaderContext: Modern dentistry treats the mouth as an ecosystem to balance, not an infection to clear. This shapes how cleaning works, why maintenance matters, and why antibiotics rarely fix it.
coreTruths.body:
## The healthy mouth is balanced, not sterile

The healthy mouth is not a sterile place. It carries a balanced community of more than 700 bacterial species, mostly working with the host rather than against it. The resident flora actually keeps outside microbes from getting a foothold [1].

## Disease is a shift in the balance, not a single invader

Periodontitis is not one invading organism. It is a shift in the community balance. The current model is called symbiosis-dysbiosis: when the biofilm is not disrupted often enough, organisms like Fusobacterium nucleatum tilt the local ecology toward pathogens such as P. gingivalis. In susceptible patients the host response that follows is what does the tissue damage [2].

## The aim of cleaning is rebalance, not sterilisation

The aim is to keep the ecology in symbiosis. Disrupting the biofilm at recall, plus good daily home care, is enough for most patients [3]. Antibiotics get used only when the ecology has tipped past what cleaning can fix on its own [4].

## Maintenance holds a balance, it does not cure an infection

Recall in a treated patient is about holding the balance, not chasing a new infection [5]. Visits start at 3–4 monthly intervals and can stretch to 6 months once things stay stable [6]. Stop maintenance and the ecology drifts back toward dysbiosis.

citations.quote: More than 700 different species can colonize the mouth and >400 species may be found in periodontal pockets. Resident oral microflora form multi-species biofilms on oral surfaces. In health there is a balanced relationship between oral microflora and the host which is mutually beneficial. The resident microflora are important in preventing colonization by exogenous microbes.

if the biofilm is not disrupted regularly, certain species such as Fusobacterium nucleatum are favoured. These enable a stronger host response and thus create the conditions that promote the development and growth of traditional pathogens such as P. gingivalis. This is known as incipient dysbiosis because in non-susceptible individuals the inflammation does not progress beyond gingivitis. However, in susceptible individuals incipient dysbiosis can trigger a host response that is excessive, resulting in collateral periodontal tissue damage.

Periodontal disease is an infection due to the presence of plaque biofilm, therefore, disruption of the plaque biofilm and control of plaque is the key to success. More complex Rx will always fail in the absence of effective plaque control.

There are few reasons to use antimicrobials in periodontal therapy. The plaque biofilm affects the response, concentration in gingival crevicular fluid is low, antibiotics have side effects, and there is the growing problem of antibiotic resistance. Antibiotics are not really justified for use in chronic periodontitis.
To avoid further attachment loss and to maintain the therapeutic benefits, long-term patients require monitoring and sometimes Rx to support their own home care.
Then maintenance visits begin at 3–4-monthly intervals and may be lengthened up to 6 months if appropriate although there is no good evidence for the ideal frequency of maintenance visits.
